doc.title: Barry Kernfeld interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, December 16, 2020

title: Innovators versus craftsmen and the critics' narrative
summary: Rowe cites Phil Woods; Kernfeld argues jazz is hurt by its obsession with newness, a myth created early by critics.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: Well said. You reminded me that when I was fortunate to interview Phil Woods he was talking about himself and he said, “Well I’m not an innovator, I’m a craftsman. You know, I learned from of course Charlie Parker and others.” But he didn’t consider himself to be doing anything really innovative. Perhaps he added his own flavor to it but it sort of goes to what you’re talking about. Who are the fountainheads of these musical styles?

And to me this is, jazz has dug itself a very deep hole and is really in trouble by putting so much emphasis on this. I have a wide range of musical interests. I go to a lot of classical concerts. I hear fabulously creative interpretations of music that’s been around for 200 years, for 400 years, for 600 years. And yet I’ve watched jazz people be so hung- up on always trying to be something new, always having his own sound, and so forth, that they end up being paralyzed. I think it’s a big problem for jazz.
And how much of it do you believe is connected to the rise in academia, in jazz education?

Oh no, I think this dates from decades before that. I think it’s a vision, it’s a myth, it’s an interpretation created by jazz critics very early on in the music as a way, as a really good handle, at that time, to write about it. Because it was continuously evolving up to the 60s, maybe the early 70s, jazz fusion. It was continuously evolving. There seemed to be a narrative that worked in describing it as a thread of this style leading to that style leading to that style. It was also a way that I feel the critics made themselves feel better about themselves because they were insiders and they knew the innovators and maybe some of the other people didn’t know the innovators and were just enjoying the imitators. You know I think it was a way of really — a petty way for people who were not making the music to live in that culture.
